expectedText:
MEAL AND REST BREAK POLICY
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

POLICY STATEMENT
Acme, Inc. maintains this Meal and Rest Break Policy to describe the meal and rest periods made available to non-exempt employees, including Jordan Lee, in the ordinary course of employment. This policy sets out when meal and rest periods are made available, the circumstances under which a meal period may be waived, and the conditions under which a meal period may be designated "on duty." This policy is a statement of Acme, Inc.'s practice; it does not itself waive, expand, or limit any right or obligation that may exist under applicable law.

THE MEAL PERIOD REQUIREMENT (FIRST AND SECOND MEAL PERIODS)
California law prohibits Acme, Inc. from employing Jordan Lee for a work period of more than 5 hours per day without providing a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if Jordan Lee's total work period for the day is no more than 6 hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee. If Jordan Lee works more than 10 hours in a day, Acme, Inc. must provide a second 30-minute meal period, except that if the total hours worked is no more than 12, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent — but only if the first meal period was not waived.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total work period per day of the employee is no more than six hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of both the employer and employee. An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than 10 hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total hours worked is no more than 12 hours, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent of the employer and the employee only if the first meal period was not waived."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 512(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 512, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=512.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 512(a)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law imposes no meal-period requirement at all, and most other states either have no meal-break statute or a far less detailed one; California's two-tier, waiver-conditioned structure is unusually specific by national comparison. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 512(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific text, though its interpretation is separately confirmed by case law cited elsewhere in this document.

THE REST PERIOD REQUIREMENT
Separately from the meal period requirement, California requires Acme, Inc. to authorize and permit Jordan Lee to take rest periods, insofar as practicable in the middle of each work period. The authorized rest time is based on total hours worked daily, at the rate of ten minutes of net rest time per four hours worked or major fraction of four hours — though a rest period need not be authorized if Jordan Lee's total daily work time is less than three and one-half hours. Authorized rest period time is counted as hours worked, and no deduction from wages may be made for it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Every employer shall authorize and permit all employees to take rest periods, which insofar as practicable shall be in the middle of each work period. The authorized rest period time shall be based on the total hours worked daily at the rate of ten (10) minutes net rest time per four (4) hours or major fraction thereof. However, a rest period need not be authorized for employees whose total daily work time is less than three and one-half (3½) hours. Authorized rest period time shall be counted as hours worked for which there shall be no deduction from wages."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 12(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 12(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This provision does not appear in the California Labor Code at all — it is a regulation adopted by the Industrial Welfare Commission, codified in Wage Order No. 4-2001 ("Professional, Technical, Clerical, Mechanical and Similar Occupations"), the general catch-all order used here because it is not industry-specific; an employer in a covered industry such as manufacturing, mercantile, or the motion picture industry would instead look to that industry's own numbered wage order, which may phrase the same 10-minutes-per-4-hours rule slightly differently. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what it says — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer. Federal law has no rest-break requirement, and most states impose none either. This is a single regulatory subdivision; no additional independent source was found for the rest-period formula itself.

THE MEAL PERIOD TIMING RULE
The California Supreme Court has held that, absent a valid waiver, § 512 requires Acme, Inc. to provide Jordan Lee a first meal period no later than the end of Jordan Lee's fifth hour of work, and a second meal period (if applicable) no later than the end of Jordan Lee's tenth hour of work.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "We conclude that, absent waiver, section 512 requires a first meal period no later than the end of an employee's fifth hour of work, and a second meal period no later than the end of an employee's 10th hour of work."
  — Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court, 53 Cal.4th 1004, 1041 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844210/brinker-restaurant-corp-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This is a holding of the California Supreme Court interpreting Labor Code § 512, one state's statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. Federal law sets no such timing requirement, having no meal-period requirement at all. This clause draws on the same opinion as the "provide, not ensure" clause elsewhere in this document (Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court); they are not independent sources of each other.

THE "PROVIDE, NOT ENSURE" STANDARD
The California Supreme Court has held that Acme, Inc.'s duty regarding meal breaks is an obligation to provide a meal period, not to ensure no work is performed during it. Acme, Inc. satisfies this obligation if it relieves Jordan Lee of all duty, relinquishes control over Jordan Lee's activities, and permits Jordan Lee a reasonable opportunity to take an uninterrupted 30-minute break, without impeding or discouraging Jordan Lee from doing so. Acme, Inc. is not obligated to police meal breaks to ensure no work is performed afterward — if Jordan Lee is bona fide relieved of duty and Acme, Inc. has relinquished control, work Jordan Lee chooses to perform during that break does not itself create premium-pay liability for Acme, Inc.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "To summarize: An employer's duty with respect to meal breaks under both section 512, subdivision (a) and Wage Order No. 5 is an obligation to provide a meal period to its employees. The employer satisfies this obligation if it relieves its employees of all duty, relinquishes, control over their activities and permits them a reasonable opportunity to take an uninterrupted 30-minute break, and does not impede or discourage them from doing so. ... On the other hand, the employer is not obligated to police meal breaks and ensure no work thereafter is performed. Bona fide relief from duty and the relinquishing of control satisfies the employer's obligations, and work by a relieved employee during a meal break does not thereby place the employer in violation of its obligations and create liability for premium pay under Wage Order No. 5, subdivision 11(B) and Labor Code section 226.7, subdivision (b)."
  — Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court, 53 Cal.4th 1004, 1040 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844210/brinker-restaurant-corp-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This is a holding of the California Supreme Court interpreting one state's statute and regulation — Labor Code § 512(a) and a wage order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer, and not a claim that this standard would apply outside California. No comparable federal standard exists, since federal law imposes no meal-period obligation to interpret. This clause draws on a single opinion (Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court); the timing-rule clause elsewhere in this document also draws on this same opinion — they are not independent sources of one another.

ON-DUTY MEAL PERIODS (NARROW EXCEPTION)
Unless Jordan Lee is relieved of all duty during a 30-minute meal period, that period is considered an "on duty" meal period and counted as time worked. California law permits an on-duty meal period only when the nature of Jordan Lee's work prevents Jordan Lee from being relieved of all duty, and only by written agreement between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee, stating that Jordan Lee may revoke the agreement in writing at any time. When an employee is employed for five hours, California's meal-period framework requires the employer to choose among: providing an off-duty meal period, obtaining a mutually agreed waiver where one hour or less will end the shift, or obtaining a written on-duty meal period agreement where circumstances permit one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless the employee is relieved of all duty during a 30 minute meal period, the meal period shall be considered an "on duty" meal period and counted as time worked. An "on duty" meal period shall be permitted only when the nature of the work prevents an employee from being relieved of all duty and when by written agreement between the parties an on-the-job paid meal period is agreed to. The written agreement shall state that the employee may, in writing, revoke the agreement at any time."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "When someone is suffered or permitted to work—i.e., employed—for five hours, an employer is put to a choice: it must (1) afford an off-duty meal period; (2) consent to a mutually agreed-upon waiver if one hour or less will end the shift; or (3) obtain written agreement to an on-duty meal period if circumstances permit."
  — Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court, 53 Cal.4th 1004, 1039-1040 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844210/brinker-restaurant-corp-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This is one state's regulatory text (an IWC wage order provision) and a passage from the California Supreme Court's decision describing that same regulatory structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. The on-duty-meal-period concept described here does not exist as a matter of federal law, which imposes no meal-period requirement to except from. This clause draws on two genuinely independent sources: a regulation (the wage order) and case law (Brinker) describing it.

THE PREMIUM PAY REMEDY FOR A MISSED MEAL OR REST PERIOD
If Acme, Inc. fails to provide Jordan Lee a meal or rest period required by an applicable statute or IWC wage order, California law requires Acme, Inc. to pay Jordan Lee one additional hour of pay at Jordan Lee's regular rate of compensation for each workday the meal or rest period is not provided. Acme, Inc. may also not require Jordan Lee to work during a meal, rest, or recovery period mandated by an applicable statute, regulation, or order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) An employer shall not require an employee to work during a meal or rest or recovery period mandated pursuant to an applicable statute, or applicable regulation, standard, or order of the Industrial Welfare Commission, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board, or the Division of Occupational Safety and Health. (c) If an employer fails to provide an employee a meal or rest or recovery period in accordance with a state law, including, but not limited to, an applicable statute or applicable regulation, standard, or order of the Industrial Welfare Commission, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board, or the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, the employer shall pay the employee one additional hour of pay at the employee's regular rate of compensation for each workday that the meal or rest or recovery period is not provided."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.7(b)-(c), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.7, subds. (b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 226.7(b)-(c)) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship. Federal law has no comparable premium-pay remedy for missed breaks, and most states with meal/rest laws do not attach an automatic one-hour-of-pay remedy the way California does. The statutory text sets one additional hour of pay for each workday a meal, rest, or recovery period is not provided — it does not, in these words, separately cap or itemize a meal-period premium against a rest-period premium as two distinct amounts; the widely applied practitioner reading is that up to two separate one-hour premiums (one for a meal violation, one for a rest violation) can apply on the same workday, but that reading is not itself quoted statutory text and is not asserted here as such. This is a single statutory section (§ 226.7); no additional independent source was found for this specific remedy language. Separately, § 226.7 currently exists in two operative versions enacted by the same 2020 session law: the version quoted here is the one operative now; a different version (expanding the definitions used for heat-illness recovery periods) becomes operative January 1, 2027.

EMPLOYEE ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed a copy of this Meal and Rest Break Policy. Jordan Lee understands that meal and rest periods are made available as described in this policy, that a meal period may be waived only under the specific circumstances described above, and that any on-duty meal period requires a separate written agreement that Jordan Lee may revoke in writing at any time.
